ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: As shown in the figure, in quadrilateral $ABCD$, $AC \perp BC$, $AB=13$, $BC=12$, $CD=3$, $AD=4$. What is the area of quadrilateral $ABCD$?
ready1_open_rewrite.raw_answer_text:
\textbf{Solution:} Given that $\because A{D}^{2}+C{D}^{2}=16+9=25=A{C}^{2}$,\\
$\therefore \angle D=90^\circ$,\\
$\therefore {S}_{\text{quadrilateral }ABCD}={S}_{\triangle ABC}+{S}_{\triangle ACD}=\frac{12\times 5}{2}+\frac{4\times 3}{2}=\boxed{36}$.

ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: As shown in the figure, in quadrilateral $ABCD$, $AC \perp BC$, $AB=13$, $BC=12$, $CD=3$, $AD=4$. What is the area of quadrilateral $ABCD$?
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The quadrilateral ABCD in the figure is composed of the triangle ABC on the right and the triangle ACD on the left; the line segment AC is drawn inside, dividing the quadrilateral into these two triangles. A is above, C is below A, B is on the right, and D is on the left; there is a right-angle mark at C, indicating that AC is perpendicular to CB. Reasoning: From the problem statement, AB=13, BC=12, and AC ⟂ BC, so triangle ABC is a right triangle with AB as the hypotenuse. By the Pythagorean theorem, AC=sqrt(13^2-12^2)=sqrt(169-144)=5. Now look at triangle ACD: AD=4, CD=3, AC=5, and 4^2+3^2=16+9=25=5^2, so triangle ACD is a right triangle with the right angle at D. The area of quadrilateral ABCD is equal to the sum of the areas of the two triangles: S_ABC=1/2·AC·BC=1/2·5·12=30, S_ACD=1/2·AD·CD=1/2·4·3=6. Therefore the total area is 30+6=36.
